limitations.describes: Per-app bandwidth — how much data each program uses
limitations.reason: Requires administrator access (ETW on Windows, BPF on macOS). JRX does not ask for administrator access, so this number does not exist for us to show.

limitations.describes: How much data went to each destination
limitations.reason: Byte counts per connection need the same elevated access. JRX can show total throughput and which services you are connected to, but not how much went to each one.

limitations.describes: Devices on a network that isolates its clients
limitations.reason: Guest and corporate Wi-Fi often block devices from seeing each other. That is the network working correctly, and no software can see through it.

limitations.describes: The identity of devices using a randomised MAC address
limitations.reason: Modern phones deliberately change their hardware address per network. JRX reports that a device is protecting its identity rather than guessing who it is.

permissions.grant_hint: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network
permissions.label: Local Network

permissions.grant_hint: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services
permissions.label: Location Services

refused.rationale: Reading packet contents would require administrator access and would expose the contents of everything you send. JRX has no capture library at all, so this cannot be switched on.
A record of every name you look up is a record of everywhere you go. JRX reads which resolvers you use, never what you asked them.
Which sites you visit is yours. JRX never reads it, from the browser or from the network.
Passwords, cookies and tokens are never read, stored, or transmitted. Nothing in JRX asks for them.
Full command lines leak file paths, tokens and arguments. JRX shows which program owns a connection, not how it was started.
